title: What to Do With Boxes of Records You Inherited at Work
summary: Inherited boxes of old files at a new job? A practical guide to inventorying, keeping, digitizing, and securely destroying records the right way.
body_markdown:
You start a new role, you are still learning where the coffee is, and then you find them. Boxes. Maybe a wall of filing cabinets, maybe a closet nobody mentioned in the interview. No index, no labels that mean anything, no context. Just a strong sense that the person who had your job before you thought all of it was important.


Now it is your problem. The good news is that inherited paper is one of the most solvable problems you will face this year. You just need a plan that keeps you out of legal trouble and ends with the records findable instead of feared. Here is that plan.


**First rule: do not shred anything yet**


The instinct is to purge. Resist it for now. The single most expensive mistake you can make with inherited records is destroying something you were legally required to keep. Retention requirements do not care that you did not create the records or that you have no idea why they exist. If a document falls under a retention rule or an active legal hold, the obligation is transferred to you the day you took the job.


So, before anything gets recycled, shredded, or hauled away, you need to know what you actually have and what the rules say about it. Everything else in this guide comes after that.


**Take a rough inventory before you touch anything**


You cannot make good decisions about records you cannot see. Do a fast first pass, not a detailed catalog. You are looking for categories and rough ages, not a line item for every folder.


As you go, note anything that jumps out as sensitive: student records, personnel files, medical or client information, anything financial. Those categories carry the strictest handling and retention rules, so you want them flagged early. By the end of an afternoon, you should be able to say, in plain terms, what kinds of records you inherited and roughly how old they are. That is enough to move to the real decision.


**Let retention schedules make the keep-or-toss call**


This is where most people freeze, because it feels like a judgment call, they are not qualified to make. Here is the relief: it usually is not a judgment call at all. A retention schedule already tells you how long a given type of record must be kept and what to do with it when that time is up.


Federal agencies work from schedules approved by the National Archives, and the[National Archives explains how records schedules work](https://www.archives.gov/records-mgmt/grs) in plain language that is useful even if you are not a federal agency. Most states publish their own retention schedules for local government, courts, and schools, and many industries have their own on top of that. The question stops being "do I feel like keeping this" and becomes "what does the schedule say for this record type?" That is a question with an actual answer.


If your organization does not have a written retention schedule yet, finding or building one is the highest-value thing you can do with these boxes. It turns every future keep-or-destroy decision from a guess into a lookup.


**Sort into three piles: keep, digitize, destroy**


With a rough inventory and a retention schedule in hand, everything you inherited falls into one of three groups.


**Keep as-is:** records still within their retention period that you genuinely need in their current form. Some documents must stay physical for legal or archival reasons. That is fine. They just need a real home, which we will get to.


**Digitize:** records you must keep but would rather not store, retrieve, and protect on paper. This is usually the biggest pile, and it is where the real payoff lives. More on it below.


**Destroy:** records that are past their retention period with no active legal hold. These can go, but "go" does not mean the office recycling bin. Anything with personal, financial, or otherwise sensitive information needs secure destruction. The[NIST guidelines for media sanitization](https://csrc.nist.gov/News/2025/guidelines-for-media-sanitization-rev-2) are the standard reference for doing this properly, and a reputable destruction process gives you a certificate of destruction as proof it was handled correctly. Keep those certificates. They are your evidence that you disposed of records the right way.


**Digitize what earns it, not everything**


Scanning is not about converting every page you own into a PDF. It is about making the records you are required to keep easy to find, share, and protect. The candidates that earn digitization are the fragile ones, at risk, frequently requested, or simply too important to leave sitting in a single paper copy in a back room.


Once records are digital, the difference is night and day. A request that used to mean an hour in the storage room becomes a search that takes seconds.[Document scanning services](https://www.intellinetics.com/solutions/scanning) handle the conversion, including the awkward formats like oversized drawings, bound books, and aging microfilm that a desktop scanner cannot touch. And if the records arrive in a mix of paper and digital,[intelligent document processing](https://intellinetics.com/solutions/intelligent-document-processing) can capture, classify, and index them automatically so they land in the right place without hours of manual data entry.


**Give the survivors a real home**


The reason you inherited a mess is almost always the same: no system, so records accumulated wherever there was space. Do not recreate that. Whatever survives the sort needs somewhere deliberate to live.


For records that must stay physical,[offsite records storage](https://www.intellinetics.com/solutions/storage) keeps them secure and retrievable without eating your office square footage and lets you pull a specific document on demand instead of driving to a storage unit. For everything digitized, a proper repository with search, access controls, and a clear structure means the next person can find a record in seconds instead of guessing which box it lives in. If you are in a school district, there are[document management solutions built specifically for K-12](https://intellinetics.com/industries/education) and the student, employee, and financial records that come with it.


**Set it up so the next person does not inherit your boxes**


You are in a rare position right now. You are seeing these records with fresh eyes, before habit sets in. Use it. Write down the retention schedule you are working on, document where different record types now live, and set a regular cadence, quarterly or annually, to review what is eligible for destruction. That last step is what keeps the boxes silently piling up again.


Do that, and the person who eventually takes your job does not inherit a closet full of mystery. They inherit a system.


**The boxes are a reset, not a punishment**


It is easy to look at inherited records as somebody else's mess dumped on your desk. Reframe it. This is a one-time chance to clean up years of accumulation and put something better in its place, and you rarely get an opening like that once the day-to-day takes over.


If the backlog is bigger than a rainy afternoon can handle, that is normal, and it is exactly the kind of project we take on so your team does not have to. You can see[how organizations have dug out from under their own paper](https://www.intellinetics.com/case-studies/) and what the other side looks like.
